chapter: New Orleans second line and Armstrong
title: Loyalty to Armstrong, his records, and Young's Creole as first band
summary: Jackson says Armstrong kept him in the band despite Collins, and mentions his tight playing on records and his lack of copies.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Oh that'd be at night time. At night time. Record or dance then? Yeah. They'd put all the lights out and play just about midnight. All the lights out and then they'd start playing the blues. Well I lived about a mile from there and I used to sit down and hear Joe this is clear. The music was right there. The outside sound. Better than the inside. And I was hearing Louis play before I ever knew it was Louis Armstrong. I didn't know it. Just like I told you I saw Louis when he first was playing. But I made a trip back down there and I heard him, I didn't know it was Louis, I wondered who he was. I was down there for a few days, I'd forgotten. Then the boys began to tell me about Louis. Some friends of mine began to tell me about Louis. Now Louis, when, he's a man like this, I'm going to tell you about Louis, I can't praise him too much. Louis put me in the band and he kept me in the band. I didn't have so many friends in that band, for different reasons. Maybe because I never cared for liquor, or maybe other reasons. I'd stick in bed and I got out of bed in New Orleans there, I stayed at the Page Hotel. The Page Hotel?

They turned that down at last. Yeah. Mike comes and tells me that I'm fired. I go over to Patterson Hotel, where Louis was, and they asked him what's the matter, Louis. I said, she'll give me a notice if I'm fired. I just stick in bed and I had a lumbago. Louis says, I put you in the band and you're going to stay in this band, I don't care what Collins said. And he and Collins had a big fuss. So I love Louis. You understand? I love Louis. I mean the reputation of being with Louis Armstrong. He lives today. People say he put me there. He used to be Louis Armstrong. I mean it's a certain lot of prestige. The last time I saw Louis here, he said, what was the same album? He said those records we made when I was with it are great. He said I played great. But I think some records I made since then, that I played better. But I've never been able to play on the records, when I just play I live my heart, because I always tighten up to a certain degree. I've never been free. You know, I never felt free. I don't know whether I was afraid of making the mistakes. Now I made some records with the Half Pint Jackson, they had them in England, and it was raving about the solo I played on it. But I don't have none of the records. I'd be so glad if I had the records. You see I didn't buy the records as these record collectors did. I threw them and every time I move or break some of them, they had to go by. I stumbled upon one of Joe Oliver's records about three years ago in the alley. And I looked at it and I saw Jeanette there and I died for it. I whispered to them and said, well you crazy? I said, don't you see this is Joe Oliver's record. I bet half of it. Oh just half of it. Half of it. Now I kept it and finally lost, you see what I'm talking about? Just half of the record. So I've got a record here now.
Maybe I can find that 15 cents for you someday.
Now here's an old term, huh?
The Southern Storm and the Devil Street Blues. See that?
That's the one, the Young's Creole.
Yeah, the Young's Creole. That's the first little band I played in.
